claims.claim: Among older spouse carers, only those reporting strain had higher adjusted 4-year mortality than non-carers.
claims.supporting_passage: participants who were providing care and experiencing caregiver strain had mortality risks that were 63% higher than noncaregiving controls (relative risk [RR], 1.63; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.00-2.65). Participants who were providing care but not experiencing strain (RR, 1.08; 95 % CI, 0.61-1.90) and those with a disabled spouse who were not providing care (RR, 1.37; 95% CI, 0.73-2.58) did not have elevated adjusted mortality rates
claims.pico_timeframe: US spouses aged 66-96 / caregiving with or without strain / non-caregivers / all-cause mortality / ~4 years
claims.safe_wording: In a 1999 US study of older people caring for a spouse, the higher death rate over 4 years was seen only in carers who said caring caused them mental or emotional strain. Carers without strain did not show a clear difference from non-carers.
claims.qualifications: Observational; adjusted for sociodemographic factors, prevalent disease and subclinical cardiovascular disease. Lower CI limit is 1.00, so borderline. Do not say 'X times more likely' or '63% higher' without saying it is a relative risk in a borderline estimate; the abstract itself says 'more likely to die'. Absolute figure available: 103 of 819 (12.6%) died in 4 years across the whole cohort, not by group. Spouse not helping despite disabled spouse: RR 1.37 (0.73 to 2.58), also not clearly raised.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Later population studies found lower mortality in carers overall.

numbers.meaning: adjusted relative risk, strained carers vs non-carers, 4 years
deaths in whole cohort at 4 years

claims.claim: The 1999 study is widely cited; five later population studies found lower mortality for carers as a whole; most carers report benefits.
claims.supporting_passage: A landmark study by Schulz and Beach that reported higher mortality rates for strained spouse caregivers has been widely cited as evidence for the physical health risks of caregiving ... However, 5 subsequent population-based studies have found reduced mortality and extended longevity for caregivers as a whole compared with noncaregiving controls. Most caregivers also report benefits from caregiving, and many report little or no caregiving-related strain.
claims.pico_timeframe: Population-based caregiver cohorts vs non-caregivers / mortality
claims.safe_wording: Later population studies found carers as a whole lived as long as or longer than non-carers. This does not show that caring protects health.
claims.qualifications: Observational. The 2015 review abstract does not explain why carers do better; the healthy-carer explanation comes from Janson 2022 (claim C18-11-c) and is stated there only as 'may be due to'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Strain still matters: Janson 2022 reports higher depression and anxiety in carers in cross-sectional studies.

claims.claim: Cochrane review: 4 trials, 753 participants, very low quality, no significant effect on carer outcomes; may reflect lack of research rather than lack of benefit.
claims.supporting_passage: Four trials are now included in the review, with 753 participants... Overall, the quality of the evidence was rated as very low. Re-analysis ... found no significant effects of respite care compared to no respite care on any caregiver variable... These results should be treated with caution, however, as they may reflect the lack of high quality research in this area rather than an actual lack of benefit.
claims.pico_timeframe: Dementia carers / respite / no respite or other / carer outcomes / varied
claims.safe_wording: A Cochrane review found only four trials of respite for dementia carers, with very low quality evidence. Taken together they did not show a clear benefit or harm. The authors say this may reflect a lack of good research rather than a lack of benefit.
claims.qualifications: 2014 review; no later Cochrane update found on PubMed search 2026-10-08. No evaluable outcomes for people with dementia. Do not say respite 'does not work'. One comparison (respite vs polarity therapy, n=38) favoured polarity therapy for perceived stress: not needed in post.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A 2026 systematic review (PMID 42568209, claim C18-13-c) reports possible carer improvements but at high or some risk of bias.

claims.claim: Respite is both a service and a psychological outcome; a positive experience depends on the carer perceiving mutual benefit.
claims.supporting_passage: Respite is understood both as a service that provides a physical break for the carer and as a psychological outcome, i.e. a mental break for the carer... The key antecedent for a positive respite experience is that the carer perceives that mutual benefit is garnered from service use.
claims.safe_wording: Research on carers' experiences suggests a break feels like a real rest when the carer believes the person they care for is benefiting too.
claims.qualifications: Concept analysis of qualitative studies, not a trial.

claims.claim: Of 217 US dementia carers, 72% said the death was a relief to them (and more than 90% believed it was a relief to the patient).
claims.supporting_passage: Seventy-two percent of caregivers reported that the death was a relief to them, and more than 90 percent reported belief that it was a relief to the patient.
claims.pico_timeframe: 217 US family carers of people with dementia in REACH / bereavement / self-report after death
claims.safe_wording: In a US study of 217 family carers of people with dementia, 72 in 100 said the death was a relief to them. This followed a long and demanding period of care: half had spent at least 46 hours a week on care in the year before the death.
claims.qualifications: Single US sample from a trial; self-reported; the study's own conclusion ties relief to 'a protracted and stressful period of caregiving'. The 'more than 90 percent believed relief to the patient' figure may read as a judgement that life with dementia is not worth living: use only with care (judge's values concern) or leave out.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Relief and grief can occur together: the abstract does not report grief, so any statement about grief is judgement, not from this source.

numbers.meaning: half of carers spent at least this in the year before death

claims.claim: Depressive symptoms fell within three months of death and were substantially lower within a year; support was needed most before death.
claims.supporting_passage: Within three months of the death, caregivers had clinically significant declines in the level of depressive symptoms, and within one year the levels of symptoms were substantially lower than levels reported while they were acting as caregivers... Intervention and support services were needed most before the patient's death.
claims.pico_timeframe: As above / depressive symptoms before vs 3 and 12 months after death
claims.safe_wording: On average, carers' depressive symptoms fell within three months of the death. The researchers concluded that carers needed support most before the death.
claims.qualifications: Group averages; some carers do not follow this pattern.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Relief and grief can coexist (judgement; not from this source).

claims.claim: In 53 studies, positive aspects of caregiving were associated with lower depression and burden and better mental health and quality of life; not with self-rated health or personal strain; mostly cross-sectional.
claims.supporting_passage: Fifty-three studies were included in the narrative synthesis. Most studies utilized a cross-sectional design... PAC was associated with lower depressive symptoms and burden. Conversely, PAC was associated with better mental health, quality of life, satisfaction with life, and competence/self-efficacy. PAC was not associated with self-rated health or personal strain/stress.
claims.safe_wording: In studies of dementia carers, finding something worthwhile in caring was linked with lower depression and burden. Most studies measured both at one time, so we do not know which comes first.

claims.claim: Lower mortality in carers compared with non-carers in longitudinal observational studies may reflect healthy people taking on caring (healthy-carer bias), and carers still show more depression and anxiety in cross-sectional studies.
claims.supporting_passage: The lower mortality rates compared to non-caregivers may be due to a healthy-carer bias in longitudinal observational studies; however, these and other potential benefits of informal caregiving deserve further attention by researchers. ... In cross-sectional evaluations, informal caregiving seemed to be associated with a higher occurrence of depression and of anxiety (ranging from 4 to 51% and 2 to 38%, respectively), pain, hypertension, diabetes and reduced quality of life.
claims.pico_timeframe: 22 low-risk-of-bias observational studies; informal carers vs non-carers; mortality and morbidity
claims.safe_wording: Carers as a whole do not die sooner than non-carers in population studies. That may be because healthier people take on caring, so it does not show that caring protects health. Carers still report more depression and anxiety.
claims.qualifications: Use 'may be due to', as the authors do. Do not say caring is good for you. Cross-sectional links cannot show cause.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Review authors do not claim the bias is proven.

claims.claim: A 2026 systematic review of 8 studies of respite care models found possible improvements in carer outcomes, but all studies were at high risk of bias or had some concerns.
claims.supporting_passage: Eight studies (three randomized controlled trials, five quasi-experimental), including 1,420 care recipients and 1,610 caregivers, were analyzed. Four studies were judged to be at high risk of bias and four had some concerns. ... Home-based and day-care programs may be associated with improvements in caregiver outcomes, although evidence regarding their cost-related outcomes remains limited. Overall, the findings should be interpreted cautiously given the generally high risk of bias among included studies.
claims.pico_timeframe: People with disability or dementia and their carers / home-based, day-care and mixed respite models / usual care or other / carer and recipient outcomes
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 review of eight studies found that respite programmes may be linked with better outcomes for carers, but every included study had a risk of bias concern, so the findings are preliminary.
claims.qualifications: Mixed population (disability and dementia); only 3 of 8 were randomised trials. Optional: may be left out so the post stays on the Cochrane gap. If used, it must not be presented as confirming benefit.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Does not overturn the Cochrane conclusion that good trials are lacking.

numbers.meaning: risk of bias in the 8 studies

claims.claim: Respite services are often under-used and acceptability can be low.
claims.supporting_passage: Respite services provide a break in the caregiving relationship for people with dementia and their carers, however they are often under-used and service acceptability can be low.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not a finding of the review (background statement)
claims.safe_wording: Do not use as a finding. If the post needs a point about what services should offer, the review's conclusions support: respite services need flexible, person-centred care with meaningful activity for people with dementia.
claims.qualifications: Background sentence only, no figure or citation opened for it.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Review is a qualitative synthesis of 23 papers; only 13 of 889 participants were people with dementia.

numbers.meaning: participants who were people with dementia in the qualitative review

claims.claim: The Care Act 2014, section 10(5), requires a carer's assessment to include whether the carer is able, and is likely to continue to be able, to provide care, and whether the carer is willing, and is likely to continue to be willing, to do so.
claims.supporting_passage: A carer's assessment must include an assessment of—(a)whether the carer is able, and is likely to continue to be able, to provide care for the adult needing care, (b)whether the carer is willing, and is likely to continue to be willing, to do so. [text as quoted in a WebSearch result summary; page not opened]
claims.safe_wording: No safe wording: no opened copy of the statute or published paper quoting it was obtained.
claims.qualifications: legislation.gov.uk blocked (WebFetch EGRESS_BLOCKED); PubMed searches for papers quoting the section returned nothing; Scite at monthly limit. Search extract alone is not enough for an essential claim (STYLE 9).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Judge's note: wording is 'able, and is likely to continue to be able' and 'willing, and is likely to continue to be willing'; the council must consider willingness, not promise to provide whatever is asked.

claims.claim: An adult carer support plan in Scotland must include the extent to which the carer is able and willing to provide care (Carers (Scotland) Act 2016).
claims.supporting_passage: The Carers (Scotland) Act 2016 places responsibility on local authorities to implement such a plan, which will be fast-tracked for carers supporting someone at the end of life.
claims.safe_wording: Drop the Scottish clause. The only opened source says the Act requires adult carer support plans, not what they must contain.
claims.qualifications: Section number and content of the plan not verified.

claims.claim: In Scotland an adult carer support plan must include emergency planning.
claims.supporting_passage: The Carers (Scotland) Act 2016 places responsibility on local authorities to implement such a plan, which will be fast-tracked for carers supporting someone at the end of life.
claims.safe_wording: Drop the clause. Say nothing about what the Scottish plan must contain.
claims.qualifications: Opened source does not mention emergency planning.

claims.claim: NICE NG150 recommends that practitioners help carers plan for emergencies.
claims.supporting_passage: [No passage found. Search summary of NG150 overview did not list emergency or contingency planning.]
claims.safe_wording: Drop the claim. Do not cite NG150 for emergency plans.

claims.claim: Some councils or carers' centres run carer emergency card or contact schemes.
claims.safe_wording: Name no scheme. If the post mentions help, say 'ask your council or local carers' centre whether they can help you write a plan', which makes no claim that a scheme exists.
claims.qualifications: Not verified; do not imply that every area has a scheme.

claims.claim: Practical advice: a carer can write a one-page plan covering the person's needs, medicines, who to call, keys and access, routine, GP and pharmacy, and give copies to the people named.
claims.supporting_passage: [Advice, not a research finding. No source opened and none needed if framed as a suggestion.]
claims.safe_wording: 'You can write a one-page plan in advance and give copies to the people named in it.' Frame as a suggestion. Do not claim that having a plan improves outcomes, reduces hospital admissions or is a legal entitlement: no evidence was found or opened for those.
claims.qualifications: Marked as judgement or advice. The medicines list and contact fields are sensible and uncontroversial but are not drawn from an opened source.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No trial or study of carer emergency plans was found on PubMed (search 2026-10-08).

candidates.reason: Strain finding (Schulz and Beach abstract) and later population findings (Roth 2015 abstract) re-opened. Healthy-carer explanation now supported by Janson 2022 as 'may be due to'. Carries borderline CI and observational caveats.

Cochrane gap and concept analysis re-opened and supported. Under-use claim is a background sentence, so it is dropped as a finding. 2026 review optional and only as preliminary. No later Cochrane update found.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep the evidence-gap framing (not proof that breaks fail) and close on the two judging questions; do not cite under-use; if the 2026 review is mentioned, say all eight studies had risk-of-bias concerns.

candidates.reason: All essential claims in the NEJM abstract. Complicated-grief figure not verified (the only grief-prevalence source in this project is a general-bereavement review, not dementia carers): omit. Use the 90 percent figure with care.
Review abstract supports the wording with the cross-sectional caveat; validated-scale claim not verified, omit. Reserve only.

Essential claim (Care Act 2014 s10(5)) only available as a search-engine extract; legislation.gov.uk could not be opened and no published paper quoting it was found. Scottish clause unverified. Per editor's guidance, replace with C18-22.
All legal, NICE and scheme claims failed verification. Supportable only as practical advice with no legal or evidence claim.
candidates.revised_angle: Practical advice: a one-page emergency plan written in advance and shared with the people named on it. No Carers (Scotland) Act clause, no NICE claim, no named emergency card scheme, no claim that plans improve outcomes or are an entitlement. Invitation line: ask your council or local carers' centre whether they can help.
